newsitem.title: USA: Home-based businesses as business opportunities.
newsitem.headline: Home-based businesses as business opportunities.

text.p: With the number of home-based businesses currently at 20 million and projected to grow at an annual rate of 5 percent, they present an almost natural market for ... other home-based businesses.
After all, who should know better what products and services such business owners need than people in similar situations?
They might -- but like their more-established competitors in corporate America, they are just as likely to need assistance themselves.

Income Opportunities magazine, that venerable purveyor of ads for franchises, business opportunities and other endeavours that often promise to put you on the fast road to riches from the comfort of your own home, recently commissioned a study on how to tap the home-based business market.

"The key question is, 'Who do small business owners turn to for advice, and what type of advertising and marketing do they respond to?'" said Donald Mazzella, managing publisher of the 40-year-old monthly. The magazine is the same one that McDonald's founder Ray Krock turned to in the 1950s when he first sought franchisees for his fledgling chain of hamburger stands.
"We realised that everyone is searching for that small marketplace, but not really getting down to what a home business person will respond to," said Mazzella.

The study, titled "The Psychology of Home Based Business," looks at what the home-based business owner needs, both at the start-up stage and on an ongoing basis. It lists several dozen "marketing opportunities" covering such areas as training and education, socialization, transportation and miscellaneous products and services.
The opportunities range from the obvious, such as providing computer and phone equipment, office supplies and the like, to time management, psychological support and home repair services.

Michael Scanlon, whose Renaissance Consortium Ltd. consulting firm prepared the report for the magazine, says home-based business owners share one basic need: "They all need help establishing their businesses and don't know where to get it."

The purveyor of a product or service to small business owners must be able to identify the product or service that the business owner needs, he says. The owners may know they need something, but they may not be able to put a finger on it and identify exactly what it is that's needed.
For example, small business owners have a tremendous need for help in terms of technical advice.

Scanlon recalled that when he set up his Chatham, N.J.-based business, "I had a hell of a time deciding on my telephone configuration. Just by chance, I found someone at Bell Atlantic who knew exactly what I needed."
But when he tried to get back to her to ask another question, he couldn't find her in the mammoth telecommunications company.
Maybe she'd left to set up her own consulting firm to help other start-ups.
"The services needed by start-ups are different from those needed by ongoing business," said Scanlon. "There has to be someone in a consulting capacity who can give them good advice."
Businesses seeking to serve this growing market need to talk to fledgling entrepreneurs.
One way for both professionals and business owners to reach a particular new-business market is to make contact with and learn more about those involved in it.

"If I wanted to reach these people, I would go to whatever professional group I wanted to reach," said Scanlon. "You have to go to the professional organisations. You have to reach them where they read, not just in their homes.
"People in those groups will go into a particular market. For example, financial executives will go into the same business -- it will just be home-based," he said.

Scanlon said he knows several lawyers and accountants who offer their services to new business owners at reduced rates. They figure they can afford to do so in the hope that once a business is established and prospering, their fees will grow with it.

The 14-page marketing report, while not all-inclusive, nonetheless offers useful insight for those hoping to tap this growing market. It is available by request via fax (212-768-3769) or by calling Mazzella at 212-642-0698.
"We believe the manual is a very good beginning tool," said Mazzella. "We're not presumptuous enough to say it will work for everyone, but we think people should read it before they go into business.
"We think it will help you avoid mistakes. Will you make them? Of course, we all do. But this might help."
